_comment: Curated, substantive intros for category and region browse pages, read by generate_pages.py. Where a key is absent the generator falls back to its auto-generated one-liner, so this can be filled in over time (counties are mostly left to the fallback for now). Keep these about genuine recurring traditions, motifs and landscape, not keyword padding. Keys: categories use the internal category id; regions use the region tag slug.

categories.beast: Britain and Ireland teem with monstrous beasts, among them the spectral black dogs of lonely lanes, the water-horses that drag riders down to drowning, and the territorial 'worms' and wild cattle of older belief. Many are bound to a single lake, moor or parish, where the creature guards a boundary or warns of a coming death.
categories.ghost: The ghosts of these islands are rarely vague. They are the wronged revenant who will not stay buried, the screaming skull that cannot be moved, the phantom coach, and the weeping or radiant figure tied to a named hall or churchyard, stories that preserve old anxieties about unquiet death, broken oaths and the boundary between the living and the dead.
categories.fairy: The fair folk of British and Irish tradition are neither tiny nor harmless: the Irish sídhe of the hollow hills, the Welsh Tylwyth Teg, the household brownies and boggarts, and the changelings left in a stolen child's place. Encounters turn on courtesy, theft, and time that runs strangely beneath the hill.
categories.water: Water holds its own people and its own perils, among them mermaids and selkies, the kelpie and each-uisge of the lochs, drowned bells and whole kingdoms sunk beneath the waves. These are the traditions of communities living by lake, river and a sea that both fed them and took them.
categories.dragon: The dragons of Britain and Ireland are usually earthbound and territorial: the wyrms and 'worms' of the north, the guardian coiled around a well or hoard, the red dragon of Welsh prophecy. Most are fixed to a named hill or village and a local hero whose slaying of the beast is still pointed out in the landscape.
categories.witch: From the trial records of North Berwick and Pendle to the cunning-folk and charmers of village life, the witch-lore of these islands mixes real persecution with belief in the evil eye, shape-shifting hares and butter that would not churn. Many places still carry the name of a woman who was accused, drowned or burned.
categories.deity: Older gods linger in the landscape, among them the Dagda and the Morrígan of Irish myth, Brigid and Lugh, the Brythonic figures of the Mabinogi, and the Romano-British deities of spring and grove. Their names survive in rivers, hills and holy wells long after their worship faded.
categories.giant: Giants are the great landscape-shapers of folk tradition: hurling the stones that became circles and causeways, gouging out valleys, and leaving their 'graves' and 'fingers' across the hills. Where ordinary people could not have raised a monument, the giants were said to have built it.
categories.location: Some places gathered folklore for thousands of years, from stone circles said to be dancers turned to stone to holy wells sought for healing, barrows that must not be disturbed, and hills where a king and his knights are said to sleep. These are the sites where the supernatural was felt to press closest to the land.
categories.hero: The legendary figures of these islands range from Arthur and his knights to Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna, from Robin Hood to the saints and outlaws whose deeds are still tied to named places. History and folklore blur: many were real, yet tradition gave them sleeping caves, buried treasure and returns foretold.
categories.pirate: Beyond the documented history, British and Irish coasts kept a folklore of pirates, privateers and wreckers, figures like Grace O'Malley and the smugglers of the Cornish and Essex shores, remembered in ballad and treasure-lore and in tales of false lights luring ships onto the rocks.

regions.england: England's folklore rarely stays still. It moves parish to parish, and each village keeps its own version of a story the next village tells differently. A black dog stalks a lonely lane in Norfolk. A worm coils around a hill in Durham. A witch's name still marks a cottage in Lancashire. Older customs survive alongside the ghosts. Derbyshire still dresses its wells with flowers each summer, and church roofs across the country carry carved green men older than the buildings around them. Much of it is tied to one exact spot: a stone, a bend in a road, a single tree still pointed out today.
regions.scotland: Scottish folklore splits along old lines of land and sea. In the Highlands, water-horses wait in lochs to drown the unwary, and the Cailleach is said to have shaped the mountains herself. Out in Orkney and Shetland, the stories turn Norse. Selkies shed their sealskins on the shore, and trows slip out of their mounds at night. Closer to the farm, a brownie might do your chores in exchange for a bowl of cream, until you insult it. The Lowlands carry a harder history: the North Berwick witch trials of the 1590s left real names attached to real accusations, and the places where they happened still remember them.
regions.wales: Welsh folklore leans heavily on the Mabinogi, the medieval collection of tales that still shapes how the country tells its own myths. Arthur belongs here too, and so does the red dragon said to have fought beneath the hill at Dinas Emrys before it ever appeared on a flag. Water carries its own stories. A lake maiden might marry a farmer at Llyn y Fan Fach and vanish the moment he breaks his promise. Fairy cattle graze mountain pasture that no one else can find. Every midwinter the Mari Lwyd, a horse's skull draped in a white sheet, still goes door to door demanding entry in verse.
regions.ireland: Ireland's oldest stories belong to the Tuatha Dé Danann, the mythical race said to have retreated into the hollow hills and become the sídhe. Their raths and cairns still dot the countryside, and farmers have avoided ploughing through some of them for generations, just in case. Two great cycles carry the human-scale heroes: Cú Chulainn and the warriors of Ulster, then Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna. A banshee's cry still means one thing in the old belief, and holy wells across the country are named for saints said to have blessed them personally.
regions.northern-ireland: Northern Ireland's folklore is the island's folklore, carried across six counties rather than stopped at a border. The sídhe, the banshee and the holy wells all belong here too, along with the Giant's Causeway, which local tradition credits to Finn McCool building a road to Scotland to fight a rival giant. Local stories add their own layer on top: haunted castles, witches remembered by name, and the restless dead who are said to walk specific stretches of road at night. Much of it, like the rest of Irish tradition, is tied to a named place you can still visit.
regions.isle-of-man: The Isle of Man has its own cast of creatures that don't quite match anything on the mainland. The Moddey Dhoo, a black dog, is said to still pad the corridors of Peel Castle. A buggane can tear the roof off a half-built church out of sheer spite. Not every spirit is hostile. A fenodyree will thresh a whole barn of corn overnight if you leave it alone and don't laugh at it. To this day, islanders greet the fairies by name when they cross the Fairy Bridge, a habit that survives from Gaelic tradition layered over centuries of Norse settlement.
regions.channel-islands: The Channel Islands sit close enough to France that their folklore leans Norman as much as British. Witches were once said to fly to a sabbat on Rocquaine Bay, and a black dog called the Tchico still supposedly haunts the lanes of Jersey at night. Guernsey keeps its own stone guardian, La Gran'mère du Chimquière, a carved menhir standing in a churchyard gate, said to grant good luck to islanders who leave her a coin. Many of the islands are named for early saints, whose small chapels and holy wells can still be found tucked into the coastline.
